title: No. 55 — The Total Number of the House of Representatives (Madison)
paragraphs: The number of which the House of Representatives is to consist forms another very interesting point of view from which this branch of the federal legislature may be considered. Scarcely any article in the whole Constitution seems to be made more worthy of attention by the weight of character and the apparent force of argument with which it has been attacked. The charges brought against it are these. First, that so small a number of representatives will be an unsafe trustee of the public interests. Second, that they will not have proper knowledge of the local circumstances of their numerous constituents. Third, that they will be drawn from that class of citizens which will sympathize least with the feelings of the mass of the people, and be most likely to aim at a permanent elevation of the few at the expense of the many. Fourth, that defective as the number will be at first, it will become more and more disproportionate by the increase of the people and the obstacles that will prevent a corresponding increase in the number of representatives.

In general it may be remarked on this subject that no political problem is less open to a precise solution than that of the most convenient number for a representative legislature. Nor is there any point on which the policy of the several States is more at variance, whether we compare their legislative assemblies directly with each other or consider the proportions they bear to their constituents. Setting aside the difference between the smallest and largest States — Delaware, whose most numerous branch consists of twenty-one representatives, and Massachusetts, where it amounts to between three and four hundred — a very considerable difference is observable among States nearly equal in population. The number of representatives in Pennsylvania is not more than one-fifth of that in Massachusetts. New York, whose population is to that of South Carolina as six to five, has little more than one-third of the number of representatives. As great a disparity prevails between Georgia and Delaware or Rhode Island. In Pennsylvania, representatives bear no greater proportion to their constituents than one for every four or five thousand. In Rhode Island, they bear a proportion of at least one for every thousand. According to the constitution of Georgia, the proportion may run as high as one to every ten electors, and must unavoidably far exceed the proportion in any of the other States.

Another general remark to be made is that the ratio between representatives and the people ought not to be the same where the people are very numerous as where they are very few. Were the representatives in Virginia regulated by the standard in Rhode Island, they would now amount to between four and five hundred, and twenty or thirty years from now, to a thousand. On the other hand, the ratio of Pennsylvania, if applied to Delaware, would reduce that State's representative assembly to seven or eight members. Nothing can be more fallacious than to base our political calculations on arithmetical principles. Sixty or seventy men may more properly be trusted with a given degree of power than six or seven. But it does not follow that six or seven hundred would be a proportionally better depository. And if we extend the supposition to six or seven thousand, the whole reasoning ought to be reversed. The truth is that in all cases at least a certain number seems necessary to secure the benefits of free consultation and discussion, and to guard against too easy a combination for improper purposes. On the other hand, the number ought to be kept within a certain limit at most, to avoid the confusion and intemperance of a multitude. In all very numerous assemblies, of whatever character, passion never fails to wrest the scepter from reason. Had every Athenian citizen been a Socrates, every Athenian assembly would still have been a mob.

It is also necessary to recall here the observations applied to the case of biennial elections. For the same reason that the limited powers of the Congress, and the control of the State legislatures, justify less frequent elections than public safety might otherwise require, the members of Congress need be less numerous than if they possessed the whole power of legislation, and were under no restraints other than the ordinary ones of other legislative bodies.

With these general ideas in mind, let us weigh the objections raised against the proposed number of members of the House of Representatives. First, it is said that so small a number cannot safely be trusted with so much power.

The number of which this branch of the legislature will consist at the start of the government will be sixty-five. Within three years a census is to be taken, when the number may be increased to one for every thirty thousand inhabitants. Every successive ten-year period the census is to be renewed, and increases may continue to be made under the above limitation. It is no extravagant guess that the first census, at the rate of one for every thirty thousand, will raise the number of representatives to at least one hundred. Counting the negroes at three-fifths, it can scarcely be doubted that the population of the United States will by then, if it does not already, amount to three million. After twenty-five years, at the projected rate of increase, the number of representatives will reach two hundred, and after fifty years, four hundred. This is a number that I presume will end all fears arising from the smallness of the body. I take for granted here what I will, in answering the fourth objection, hereafter show — that the number of representatives will be increased from time to time in the manner provided by the Constitution. On the contrary supposition, I would admit the objection has very great weight indeed.

The true question to be decided then is this. Is the smallness of the number, as a temporary regulation, dangerous to public liberty? Will sixty-five members for a few years, and a hundred or two hundred for a few more, be a safe depository for a limited and well-guarded power of legislating for the United States? I must own that I could not give a negative answer to this question without first erasing every impression I have received about the present genius of the people of America, the spirit that animates the State legislatures, and the principles incorporated into the political character of every class of citizens. I cannot conceive that the people of America, in their present temper, or under any circumstances that can soon arise, will choose, and every second year repeat the choice of, sixty-five or a hundred men disposed to form and pursue a scheme of tyranny or treachery. I cannot conceive that the State legislatures, which must feel so many motives to watch the federal legislature, and which possess so many means of counteracting it, would fail to detect or defeat a conspiracy of the latter against the liberties of their common constituents. I am equally unable to conceive that there are now, or can be in any short time, in the United States, any sixty-five or hundred men capable of recommending themselves to the choice of the people at large, who would either desire or dare, within the short space of two years, to betray the solemn trust committed to them. What change of circumstances, time, and a fuller population of our country may produce requires a prophetic spirit to declare, which I do not pretend to have. But judging from the circumstances now before us, and from their probable state within a moderate period of time, I must declare that the liberties of America cannot be unsafe in the number of hands proposed by the federal Constitution.

From what quarter can the danger come? Are we afraid of foreign gold? If foreign gold could so easily corrupt our federal rulers and enable them to ensnare and betray their constituents, how has it happened that we are at this time a free and independent nation? The Congress that conducted us through the Revolution was a less numerous body than its successors will be. They were not chosen by, nor responsible to, their fellow-citizens at large. Though appointed yearly, and recallable at pleasure, they were generally continued for three years, and before the ratification of the federal articles, for a still longer term. They held their consultations always under the veil of secrecy. They had the sole transaction of our affairs with foreign nations. Throughout the war they had the fate of their country more in their hands than will ever, we hope, be the case with our future representatives. Given the greatness of the prize at stake and the eagerness of the party that lost it, it may well be supposed that the use of means other than force would not have been scrupled. Yet we know by happy experience that the public trust was not betrayed. Nor has the purity of our public councils in this respect ever suffered, even from the whispers of slander.

Is the danger feared from the other branches of the federal government? But where are the means to be found by the President, or the Senate, or both? Their official salaries, we may presume, will not, and without a previous corruption of the House of Representatives cannot, more than suffice for very different purposes. Their private fortunes, since they must all be American citizens, cannot possibly be sources of danger. The only means they can possess, then, will be in the dispensing of appointments. Is it here that suspicion rests her charge? Sometimes we are told that this fund of corruption is to be exhausted by the President in subduing the virtue of the Senate. Now, the fidelity of the other House is to be the victim. The improbability of such a mercenary and treacherous combination among the several members of government — standing on as different foundations as republican principles will well admit, and at the same time accountable to the society over which they are placed — ought alone to quiet this apprehension. But fortunately, the Constitution has provided a still further safeguard. Members of Congress are made ineligible for any civil offices that may be created, or whose salaries may be increased, during the term of their election. No offices, therefore, can be dealt out to existing members except such as may become vacant by ordinary casualties. To suppose that these would be sufficient to purchase the guardians of the people, selected by the people themselves, is to renounce every rule by which events ought to be calculated, and to substitute an indiscriminate and unbounded jealousy with which all reasoning must be vain. The sincere friends of liberty who give themselves up to the extravagances of this passion are not aware of the injury they do their own cause. As there is a degree of depravity in mankind that requires a certain degree of caution and distrust, so there are other qualities in human nature that justify a certain portion of esteem and confidence. Republican government presupposes the existence of these qualities to a higher degree than any other form. Were the pictures drawn by the political jealousy of some among us faithful likenesses of human character, the inference would be that there is not sufficient virtue among men for self-government, and that nothing less than the chains of despotism can restrain them from destroying and devouring one another.
